Empirical Research Plan  
“How do historical institutions established during the colonial period affect current economic development across countries?”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Instrumental‐Variables (IV) / Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)

Why IV?  
•  The causal object is the long-run effect of institutional quality (endogenous) on contemporary GDP per capita.  
•  Institutions are not randomly assigned; they are jointly determined with many unobservables (culture, geography, pre-colonial prosperity).  
•  European settler mortality rates provide a plausibly exogenous source of variation that shaped the type of colonial institutions but is predetermined with respect to today’s outcomes.  
•  The data are cross-sectional at the country level, so panel-based designs (DID, event study) are infeasible; RDD has no natural cutoff.  

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Endogenous “treatment” variable  
  InstQualityᵢ  = quality of historical / early-20ᵗʰ-century institutions in country i (e.g., Polity constraint on executive, protection against expropriation, or similar index). It is measured on a continuous scale; higher = more inclusive.  

Instrument  
  log(SettlerMortalityᵢ)  = log of annual European settler deaths per 1,000 at the time of first permanent settlement (17ᵗʰ-19ᵗʰ C.).  

Control / counterfactual  
  Countries with high settler mortality that received extractive institutions act as the implicit control for countries with low mortality (inclusive institutions), once the instrument is used.  

Timing  
  Not applicable; all variables are cross-sectional and time-invariant for our purposes.  

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance: Settler mortality strongly predicts institutional quality.  
  Plausibility: Historical accounts document that Europeans avoided permanent settlement in high-mortality environments and instead set up extractive regimes, while healthier colonies received settler states and inclusive institutions.  

A2. Exclusion (exogeneity): Conditional on covariates, settler mortality affects current GDP only through its impact on institutions—not through direct channels (e.g., persistent disease environment).  
  Plausibility: The main competing channel is geography/disease that might still hamper modern productivity. We will empirically mitigate this by controlling for geography and present-day disease environment, and by showing that mortality has no residual effect once institutions are controlled for.  

A3. Monotonicity: Lower settler mortality never led Europeans to create *worse* institutions (no “defiers”).  
  Plausibility: Historical narratives support a monotonic mapping from mortality risk to settlement effort/institution type.  

A4. SUTVA: A country’s institutional trajectory does not affect another’s GDP through spillovers that correlate with mortality.  
  Plausibility: Inter-country spillovers exist (trade, conflict) but are unlikely to be systematically related to initial settler mortality once continent dummies are included.  

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Geography/disease directly lowers modern GDP (violates exclusion).  
  Mitigation: Add controls—absolute latitude, distance to coast, tropical climate share, malaria ecology index, soil quality, natural-resource endowment. Show that coefficients on institutions remain stable. Perform placebo regressions where mortality is used to predict modern GDP conditional on institutions; expect coefficient ≈ 0.  

T2. Measurement error in historical mortality or institution index → weak instrument / attenuation.  
  Mitigation: (i) Use log mortality to reduce skewness; (ii) report first-stage F-statistic; (iii) try alternative mortality sources (troop mortality, bishop mortality) as instruments; (iv) use LIML as robustness.  

T3. Sample selection—only colonies with data survive; survivorship correlated with outcomes.  
  Mitigation: (i) Show summary stats for included vs. excluded colonies; (ii) re-weight observations by population or inverse-probability weights; (iii) conduct sensitivity bounds (Oster or Altonji) to assess impact of selection on coefficient stability.  

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- 1. Load packages ----
library(readr)     # data import
library(dplyr)     # wrangling
library(fixest)    # fast IV estimation with clustered SEs
library(AER)       # for first-stage F-stat
library(sandwich)  # robust vcov
library(lmtest)    # Wald tests

# ---- 2. Import data ----
df <- read_csv("colonial_origins.csv")   # filename placeholder

# ---- 3. Variable construction ----
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    lGDP_pc_1995 = log(GDP_pc_1995),
    lMortality   = log(Settler_Mortality),
    # institution index already in data as 'Instit_Index'
    Tropics      = Tropic_Share / 100,
    lPopDensity1500 = log(PopDensity_1500 + 1)
  ) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(lGDP_pc_1995), !is.na(Instit_Index), !is.na(lMortality))

# ---- 4. Main 2SLS specification ----
# 2nd stage: log GDP on institutions + controls
# 1st stage: institutions on log mortality + controls
iv_formula <- lGDP_pc_1995 ~ Instit_Index + 
                latitude + Tropics + lPopDensity1500 + Continent_FE |
              lMortality   + 
                latitude + Tropics + lPopDensity1500 + Continent_FE

iv_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = df, cluster = "Continent_FE")
summary(iv_main, stage = 1)      # prints both stages and F-stat

# First-stage F-stat manually (should exceed 10)
library(car)
iv_stage1 <- feols(Instit_Index ~ lMortality + latitude + Tropics + 
                     lPopDensity1500 + Continent_FE, 
                   data = df, cluster = "Continent_FE")
waldtest(iv_stage1, ~lMortality) 

# ---- 5. Robustness: add malaria ecology & drop outliers ----
df2 <- df %>% filter(lMortality < quantile(lMortality, 0.99))  # drop top 1% mortality
iv_formula_rb <- update(iv_formula, . ~ . + Malaria_Ecology)
iv_rb <- feols(iv_formula_rb, data = df2, cluster = "Continent_FE")
etable(iv_main, iv_rb, se = "cluster")

# ---- 6. Placebo: effect of mortality on GDP after controlling for institutions ----
placebo <- feols(lGDP_pc_1995 ~ lMortality + Instit_Index + latitude + Tropics +
                   lPopDensity1500 + Continent_FE, data = df, 
                 cluster = "Continent_FE")
summary(placebo)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Prior: More inclusive institutions → higher present-day GDP per capita.  
Magnitude (rough guide from theory and previous stylised facts):  
•  A one-standard-deviation increase in institutional quality (≈ 1 point on a 7-point index) raises log GDP per capita by about 0.4–0.6 (≈ 50–80 %).  
•  First-stage: Going from 90th to 10th percentile of log settler mortality (~3.5 → 1.5) increases the institution index by ~1.2 points.  

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  

C1 – Strong first stage (F > 10) ………………… 1  
C2 – Plausible exclusion restriction ………… 0.7  
C3 – Monotonicity / no defiers ……………….. 1  
C4 – No interference (SUTVA) ………………… 0.8  
C5 – Accurate, reliable data ……………………. 0.9  

Overall ≈ 4.4 / 5 ⇒ fairly strong but not ironclad; geography-based exclusion remains the main concern.
